title: Course Description and Objectives
text:
Course Description
How environmental and safety hazards influence public health and sustainability. Multiple perspectives on water, air, and solid waste pollution, sustainability and public safety issues.
This class is focused on providing you an introduction to the relationship between the environment and health; an introduction to environmental health; and, most importantly, an opportunity for you to reflect on your own values, learning, and goals in the context of your existence and the planet that you live on.



General Education
This course meets the requirements of Area E – Lifelong Learning.



Prerequisites
None.



Course Modality
Asynchronous Online



Course Student Learning Outcomes (SLOs)

Further their own critical self-understanding and acquire the knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary to engage and reflect in learning and self-development practices.
Develop strategies to be integrated physiological, socio-cultural, and psychological beings to promote a holistic awareness of lifelong learning throughout their lives.
Develop themselves as responsible citizens, employees and employers, family members, and members of the global society.
Actively apply and participate in developing a lifelong commitment to health for both personal well-being (such as physical, financial, emotional, intellectual, spiritual, social/interpersonal, and/or environmental aspects) and societal responsibility.
Discuss concepts of sustainability associated with natural resources and human population.
Explore people’s attitudes and motivations to change consumptive practices to preserve natural resources.
Characterize the health outcomes of exposure to environmental pollutants, including air, water, and food.
Understand the importance of safety in protecting the public and workers from various hazards at home and workplaces.
Review careers available in environmental health and safety.

title: Module 3 - System Framing and Initial Map (3 Weeks)
text:
Element Selection
You are provided with a structured list of system elements representing major domains of the U.S. health care and public health system, including:

care providers
federal and state policy / enforcement and accountability
financing / insurance
funding
payment models
pharmaceuticals and devices
public health
structural determinants
structural inequities

title: CSV Explainer
text:
A CSV file is a simple way to store a table of data in a plain-text file. CSV stands for Comma-Separated Values. It’s one of the most common formats for sharing data because it works across tools (Excel, Google Sheets, R, Python, etc.) and doesn’t depend on special spreadsheet formatting.
In this course, CSVs are the default way you’ll receive and share datasets.


A CSV is:

A table where each row is a record (an observation)
Each column is a variable (a field)
Values in a row are typically separated by commas

A CSV is not:

A formatted spreadsheet (no colors, merged cells, multiple tabs, formulas, charts, etc.)
A “smart” file that knows your data types
A safe place to rely on formatting (because it doesn’t store formatting)

A CSV is essentially a text file that looks like this:
city,date,temp_c
Oakland,2025-06-01,22.3
Oakland,2025-06-02,19.8
The first line is often the header row (column names).



CSV is popular because:

It’s easy to share and open in almost any tool
It’s transparent (you can open it in a text editor and see what’s inside)
It plays well with data analysis workflows
It avoids some of the hidden behaviors of spreadsheet formats

The downside is that CSV is also unforgiving: small issues can break it or change what it means.





Excel may silently change your data:

Turning IDs like 001234 into 1234 (leading zeros vanish)
Converting strings into dates (e.g., 3-4 becomes Mar-04)
Changing long numbers (loss of precision)

Rule of thumb: If a column contains IDs, zip codes, or codes, treat it as text—not numbers.



Because commas separate values, text fields that contain commas can cause problems unless they’re quoted.
Example:
name,notes
Smith,"works in Oakland, CA"
If quotes are missing, the comma in “Oakland, CA” can be misread as a separator.



A missing value in a CSV often appears as:

An empty cell: Oakland,,22.3
A placeholder like NA, N/A, null, -, or 999

Missingness matters. It is often a real feature of the system, not just an annoyance.



These values might be meant to represent the same thing:

CA, California, Calif., ca

Cleaning often means making categories consistent, but that requires judgment.



These are common in “human-facing spreadsheets,” but they make data hard to analyze.
A clean dataset usually has:

One header row
No merged cells
No totals rows inside the dataset
No embedded notes inside the data grid

If you need notes, keep them outside the dataset or in a separate documentation file.







Save an untouched copy of the original CSV.
Do cleaning on a copy.
Avoid overwriting your only source.




After opening and saving a CSV, quickly verify:

Column count stayed the same
Column names didn’t shift
No surprise conversions (dates, IDs, leading zeros)




Using Excel’s import tools can let you specify data types and prevent unwanted conversions.




Try this on any CSV you have:

Open the CSV in your tool of choice.
Answer these questions in plain language:

What does each row represent?
What does each column represent?
Which columns are numeric? Which are categories? Which are identifiers?
Do you see missing values? If so, how are they represented?
Do any values look inconsistent (spelling, capitalization, categories)?

Save a cleaned copy (new filename) and confirm the structure didn’t change unexpectedly.

If you can do this, you are in good stead for the data work in this course.



A CSV is a plain-text table. That simplicity is its power—and also why it needs to be handled carefully. The goal is not to make the file look nice, but to preserve meaning while making the data usable and trustworthy.

title: AI Explainer
text:
What this page is for. Module 5 and Module 6 ask you to use AI adversarially — to challenge your own reasoning rather than help you write it. That’s a different skill than using AI to brainstorm or draft, and it’s easy to do badly without realizing it: either too trusting (accepting whatever the AI says as correct) or too dismissive (ignoring a real problem because the AI’s tone was blunt). This page is about doing it well.



An AI tool like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini predicts plausible next words based on patterns in enormous amounts of text. That’s a genuinely useful capability — it can hold a lot of context, connect ideas quickly, and describe unfamiliar concepts clearly. It is not:

A mind that knows your system. It has no access to your team’s map, your research, or your health problem unless you put that information in front of it. It cannot “remember” your project between conversations unless you paste the relevant material back in each time.
A source of truth. It can state a fabricated citation, an invented statistic, or a false claim about the U.S. health care system with exactly the same confident tone it uses for something true. This is not a rare glitch — it’s a structural feature of how these tools generate text. Fluent and confident is not the same as correct.
A peer, a professor, or an author. It doesn’t have a stake in your grade, a professional judgment about your reasoning, or authorship responsibility for what it produces. You do. See the Class AI Policy for exactly where that responsibility line sits in this course.
Neutral or objective by default. These tools tend toward agreement — telling you your idea is reasonable, your map is solid, your causal claim makes sense — unless you specifically instruct them not to. Left to their own devices, they are better at being agreeable than at being rigorous.

The practical upshot: treat AI output the way you’d treat a claim from an anonymous internet source — plausible-sounding, sometimes genuinely useful, and never something you cite or rely on without checking it yourself.



Narrow the task. Don’t hand an AI your whole system map and ask “is this good?” — that produces a vague, generically positive answer. Give it one specific causal claim, one relationship, one assumption, and ask it to test that one thing. Small, concrete inputs produce answers you can actually evaluate.
Ask it to disagree with you. Because these tools default toward agreement, you have to explicitly instruct them to look for problems: “Challenge this claim. What would have to be true for it to be wrong? What’s the weakest part of this reasoning?” A prompt that just asks “does this make sense?” will usually get “yes, that makes sense” whether or not it actually does.
Verify anything it tells you. If an AI cites a source, a statistic, or a fact about how the health care system works, check it against a source from Research Resources before you rely on it. If it can’t be verified, treat the claim as unsupported — the same standard you’d apply to an unsupported claim in your own map.
Iterate — don’t accept the first answer as a verdict. Push back. Ask it to defend its critique, or to explain its reasoning the way you’d ask a classmate to explain theirs. A single AI response is a draft challenge, not a ruling.
Learn to tell a real gap from a superficial one. This is the actual skill being graded in Modules 5–6. AI sometimes surfaces a genuine weakness you hadn’t seen. It sometimes produces a critique that sounds sophisticated but doesn’t actually apply to your specific claim, or restates your claim back at you with a skeptical tone and calls that a challenge. Distinguishing the two is your job, not the AI’s — and it’s exactly what your written response is evaluated on.



A skill, in this context, is a written set of instructions you give an AI in advance so it evaluates things the same way every time, instead of you improvising a new prompt each time and hoping it asks the right questions. Think of it as a checklist or rubric you hand the AI, rather than a single question.
Why this matters for Module 6. An ad hoc prompt like “critique my memo” tends to produce a vague, generically encouraging response. A well-built skill that says specifically what to check for — unsupported causal claims, unjustified polarity, feedback loops that don’t actually close, elements that should be stocks but read like one-time events — produces a critique you can actually act on. Module 6 asks you to draft this skill yourself and grades it on its own rigor, because writing a good skill requires the same understanding of what makes causal reasoning strong or weak that the underlying assignment is trying to teach.
How to draft a skill that’s actually rigorous:

Name specific failure modes, not vague quality checks. “Check if this is good” produces nothing useful. “Check whether each causal arrow has a stated mechanism, whether polarity is justified rather than asserted, and whether any named feedback loop actually closes back on its starting element” produces something checkable.
Use the course’s own vocabulary. Stocks vs. flows, polarity, feedback loops, endogenous vs. exogenous, delays — instructing the AI to evaluate using these specific concepts (from Systems Thinking Foundations) means it’s applying the same standard you’re being graded on, not some generic notion of “good writing.”
Explicitly instruct it not to just agree. Include a line like “actively look for the weakest link in this reasoning; do not simply confirm the strongest part.” Without this, the default agreeableness bias described above will produce a soft critique regardless of how the rest of the skill is worded.
Test your own skill before you submit it. Run it against your memo, and then run it against something you know is weak (a claim with no mechanism, a made-up polarity). If your skill gives both a passing grade, it isn’t rigorous enough — and a critique skill written to be gentle is graded down on its own terms, not just on the response it produces.

A rough template — deliberately from an unrelated domain, so you can see the structure without being able to just paste it into your own memo with the blanks filled in:

You are reviewing the reasoning behind a workout plan for [describe the specific section — e.g., “the choice of exercises for week 3”]. For each claim, check:

Is there a stated physiological mechanism, or is a result being asserted without explaining why it would happen?
Is the claimed effect (build muscle, improve endurance, prevent injury) justified with a reason, or just labeled?
Does every claimed cause-and-effect chain actually close — does the proposed mechanism plausibly lead all the way to the stated outcome, with no missing step?
Are any recommended changes performative (just “do more cardio,” “eat more protein”) without explaining the specific mechanism of improvement?

Do not soften your critique or default to agreement. Identify the single weakest claim in this plan and explain specifically why it’s weak.

Notice the shape: name the failure modes, force the critique to use the domain’s own vocabulary (here, physiology terms — for your memo, systems-thinking terms), and explicitly forbid soft-pedaling. That shape is what transfers to your own skill. The workout-plan content itself doesn’t — you have to build the systems-thinking version yourself, using Systems Thinking Foundations’s vocabulary the way this template uses exercise science’s.



Common AI failure modes to watch for, specifically:

Hallucinated citations — a source that sounds real, formatted correctly, and doesn’t exist (or exists but doesn’t say what’s claimed).
Fabricated statistics — a precise-sounding number with no traceable origin.
Confident tone regardless of accuracy — AI does not signal uncertainty the way a careful human source would; a wrong answer and a right one can read identically.
Sycophancy — agreeing with whatever you already believe unless explicitly told to do otherwise (this is why Section 2 and Section 3 both emphasize instructing it to disagree).
Shallow “critique” — restating your own claim back to you in a skeptical tone without actually identifying a specific mechanism-level problem. This can look like a real critique at a glance; check whether it names something concrete about your claim or could have been generated for almost any claim.

The grading principle, restated one more time because it’s the whole point: your written response to the critique — what you agreed with, what you pushed back on, and why — is what’s graded. Not the AI exchange itself, and not whether you used AI at all. A thoughtful response to a mediocre AI critique is worth more than a transcript of a great one with no engagement attached.
Disclosure still applies outside this mechanism. Using AI adversarially for the Module 5–6 exercises is built into the assignment design and doesn’t need a separate disclosure. If you use AI elsewhere in your work on this course — brainstorming, drafting, checking clarity — the normal disclosure expectations in the Syllabus still apply.
This is assignment-embedded use, not exam use. AI may not be used during Exam 1 or the Final Exam, full stop — see the Class AI Policy.



Before your Module 5 or Module 6 submission, see if you can answer these honestly:

Did I give the AI a specific, narrow claim to test — not my whole map or memo at once?
Did I explicitly instruct it to challenge me, or did I just ask a neutral question and take whatever it said?
Did I check any citation, statistic, or factual claim it made before treating it as true?
Can I tell the difference between a critique that names something specific and wrong, versus one that just sounds skeptical?
If I drafted a critique skill: did I test it against something I know is weak, to confirm it doesn’t just pass everything?
Is my written response — not the AI transcript — actually doing the reasoning work this assignment is grading?

If you can answer yes to these, you’re using AI the way this course’s adversarial-critique mechanism is designed for.

The practical upshot: treat AI output the way you’d treat a claim from an anonymous internet source — plausible-sounding, sometimes genuinely useful, and never something you cite or rely on without checking it yourself.

title: AI Explainer
text:
Narrow the task. Don’t hand an AI your whole system map and ask “is this good?” — that produces a vague, generically positive answer. Give it one specific causal claim, one relationship, one assumption, and ask it to test that one thing. Small, concrete inputs produce answers you can actually evaluate.
Ask it to disagree with you. Because these tools default toward agreement, you have to explicitly instruct them to look for problems: “Challenge this claim. What would have to be true for it to be wrong? What’s the weakest part of this reasoning?” A prompt that just asks “does this make sense?” will usually get “yes, that makes sense” whether or not it actually does.
Verify anything it tells you. If an AI cites a source, a statistic, or a fact about how the health care system works, check it against a source from Research Resources before you rely on it. If it can’t be verified, treat the claim as unsupported — the same standard you’d apply to an unsupported claim in your own map.
Iterate — don’t accept the first answer as a verdict. Push back. Ask it to defend its critique, or to explain its reasoning the way you’d ask a classmate to explain theirs. A single AI response is a draft challenge, not a ruling.
Learn to tell a real gap from a superficial one. This is the actual skill being graded in Modules 5–6. AI sometimes surfaces a genuine weakness you hadn’t seen. It sometimes produces a critique that sounds sophisticated but doesn’t actually apply to your specific claim, or restates your claim back at you with a skeptical tone and calls that a challenge. Distinguishing the two is your job, not the AI’s — and it’s exactly what your written response is evaluated on.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: AI Explainer
text:
A skill, in this context, is a written set of instructions you give an AI in advance so it evaluates things the same way every time, instead of you improvising a new prompt each time and hoping it asks the right questions. Think of it as a checklist or rubric you hand the AI, rather than a single question.
Why this matters for Module 6. An ad hoc prompt like “critique my memo” tends to produce a vague, generically encouraging response. A well-built skill that says specifically what to check for — unsupported causal claims, unjustified polarity, feedback loops that don’t actually close, elements that should be stocks but read like one-time events — produces a critique you can actually act on. Module 6 asks you to draft this skill yourself and grades it on its own rigor, because writing a good skill requires the same understanding of what makes causal reasoning strong or weak that the underlying assignment is trying to teach.
How to draft a skill that’s actually rigorous:

Name specific failure modes, not vague quality checks. “Check if this is good” produces nothing useful. “Check whether each causal arrow has a stated mechanism, whether polarity is justified rather than asserted, and whether any named feedback loop actually closes back on its starting element” produces something checkable.
Use the course’s own vocabulary. Stocks vs. flows, polarity, feedback loops, endogenous vs. exogenous, delays — instructing the AI to evaluate using these specific concepts (from Systems Thinking Foundations) means it’s applying the same standard you’re being graded on, not some generic notion of “good writing.”
Explicitly instruct it not to just agree. Include a line like “actively look for the weakest link in this reasoning; do not simply confirm the strongest part.” Without this, the default agreeableness bias described above will produce a soft critique regardless of how the rest of the skill is worded.
Test your own skill before you submit it. Run it against your memo, and then run it against something you know is weak (a claim with no mechanism, a made-up polarity). If your skill gives both a passing grade, it isn’t rigorous enough — and a critique skill written to be gentle is graded down on its own terms, not just on the response it produces.

A rough template — deliberately from an unrelated domain, so you can see the structure without being able to just paste it into your own memo with the blanks filled in:

You are reviewing the reasoning behind a workout plan for [describe the specific section — e.g., “the choice of exercises for week 3”]. For each claim, check:

Is there a stated physiological mechanism, or is a result being asserted without explaining why it would happen?
Is the claimed effect (build muscle, improve endurance, prevent injury) justified with a reason, or just labeled?
Does every claimed cause-and-effect chain actually close — does the proposed mechanism plausibly lead all the way to the stated outcome, with no missing step?
Are any recommended changes performative (just “do more cardio,” “eat more protein”) without explaining the specific mechanism of improvement?

Do not soften your critique or default to agreement. Identify the single weakest claim in this plan and explain specifically why it’s weak.

Notice the shape: name the failure modes, force the critique to use the domain’s own vocabulary (here, physiology terms — for your memo, systems-thinking terms), and explicitly forbid soft-pedaling. That shape is what transfers to your own skill. The workout-plan content itself doesn’t — you have to build the systems-thinking version yourself, using Systems Thinking Foundations’s vocabulary the way this template uses exercise science’s.

title: AI Explainer
text:
Common AI failure modes to watch for, specifically:

Hallucinated citations — a source that sounds real, formatted correctly, and doesn’t exist (or exists but doesn’t say what’s claimed).
Fabricated statistics — a precise-sounding number with no traceable origin.
Confident tone regardless of accuracy — AI does not signal uncertainty the way a careful human source would; a wrong answer and a right one can read identically.
Sycophancy — agreeing with whatever you already believe unless explicitly told to do otherwise (this is why Section 2 and Section 3 both emphasize instructing it to disagree).
Shallow “critique” — restating your own claim back to you in a skeptical tone without actually identifying a specific mechanism-level problem. This can look like a real critique at a glance; check whether it names something concrete about your claim or could have been generated for almost any claim.

The grading principle, restated one more time because it’s the whole point: your written response to the critique — what you agreed with, what you pushed back on, and why — is what’s graded. Not the AI exchange itself, and not whether you used AI at all. A thoughtful response to a mediocre AI critique is worth more than a transcript of a great one with no engagement attached.
Disclosure still applies outside this mechanism. Using AI adversarially for the Module 5–6 exercises is built into the assignment design and doesn’t need a separate disclosure. If you use AI elsewhere in your work on this course — brainstorming, drafting, checking clarity — the normal disclosure expectations in the Syllabus still apply.
This is assignment-embedded use, not exam use. AI may not be used during Exam 1 or the Final Exam, full stop — see the Class AI Policy.

Did I give the AI a specific, narrow claim to test — not my whole map or memo at once?
Did I explicitly instruct it to challenge me, or did I just ask a neutral question and take whatever it said?

Individual Assignments

Exam 1 - Window: September 14–18, 2026
Exam 1 covers Module 2 (Systems Thinking Foundations) and is on Canvas. It consists of multiple choice and multiple answer questions. This exam assesses your ability to reason about systems, not to memorize terms or definitions.
You will be asked to analyze short system descriptions and, in some cases, simple diagrams. All necessary information is provided in each question. Focus on how elements interact over time, including feedback loops, delays, and system boundaries.
The exam is fully auto-graded and consists of multiple-choice and multiple-select questions. You may move freely between questions and change your answers before submitting. You have 75 minutes to complete the exam.
The time limit is designed so that students who understand the material can complete the exam comfortably without external resources. Careful reading and clear reasoning are more important than speed.

Academic Integrity and Late / Missed Exam Policy
This exam must be completed independently.
The structure and timing of the exam are intentionally designed so that external tools, shared answers, or AI-generated responses are unlikely to be helpful. Using such tools undermines the purpose of the assessment and may result in answers that are internally inconsistent or incorrect.
You are expected to rely on your own reasoning and understanding. The goal is not to catch mistakes, but to establish a clear baseline for your work in the rest of the course.
If you miss your exam, you may take the exam late. The exam time will be reduced and there will be 5% reduction of the final score. To take an exam late, after missing your exam, you must contact me within two days. If I do not hear from you after two days and you have missed an exam, you may not take a late exam.



Final Exam - Open Window During Finals Week (Dec 13–19)
There is no single fixed date/time for the Final Exam. It will be open for you to complete at any point during Finals Week, Dec 13–19.
The final exam is an individual assessment of your understanding of the organization and financing of the U.S. health care system. The exam is primarily multiple choice and focuses on explanation and reasoning rather than memorization. Questions will ask you to interpret short scenarios and identify which explanations or outcomes are most consistent with how the U.S. health care system is structured, including financing, payment, governance, access, and equity. You are not expected to recall exhaustive factual detail or definitions; instead, you are expected to demonstrate the ability to connect system components, recognize constraints and tradeoffs, and explain why certain patterns or outcomes persist. The exam is designed to reward clear reasoning and synthesis developed over the course of the term rather than rote recall.

A note on questions, confusion, and communication
This course is designed to challenge how you think about public health problems. As a result, there will be times when you feel uncertain, confused, or unsure how to proceed — especially early in the term.
That experience is expected.
In this course, confusion is not a failure and it is not something to wait out. It is often the first signal that you are engaging with systems thinking rather than memorization or procedure.
You do not need to have a fully formed question in order to reach out. “I’m not sure what I’m missing,” “I don’t know how to improve this,” or “I feel stuck” are all sufficient reasons to contact me or come to office hours.
Waiting until the end of the term to raise questions makes it much harder to resolve them. Early, partial, and even inarticulate questions are strongly encouraged and will be treated as a normal part of learning in this course.






TipImportant



If you feel confused and don’t know what to ask yet — that is the moment to reach out. You don’t need a polished question. Uncertainty is a valid reason to communicate in this course.

Technical Problems and Documentation Policy
This course uses multiple platforms with distinct roles. It is your responsibility to use them appropriately and to report technical problems promptly and through the correct channel. ### Canvas Technical Failures Issues involving Canvas access, submissions, quizzes, or grades must be reported to me immediately. After notifying me, you are expected to contact campus IT Services (ITS) and follow their procedures. Documentation from ITS may be required. Canvas problems reported after a deadline, without prior notice or documentation, will not be accommodated. ### Course Website Issues Problems accessing or using the course website materials should be reported directly to me. This platform is part of the course infrastructure, but it is not centrally supported by the university. Timely communication is required. ### Personal Technical Problems Problems with your own computer, internet connection, software, file corruption, browser issues, time zone settings, or general device failure are not grounds for extensions or exceptions. You are expected to maintain reliable access to a functioning computer and internet connection for an online course. ### Timing and Documentation Technical issues must be reported as soon as they occur. Waiting until or after a deadline to report a problem substantially limits what, if anything, can be done. Screenshots, error messages, timestamps, or ITS documentation may be required. ### Bottom Line This is an asynchronous online course. Managing your technology is part of managing the course. Legitimate system failures will be handled fairly when reported promptly and through the correct channel. Personal technical failures remain your responsibility. ## Required Technical Competencies
Most students can develop or refresh these skills on their own with a bit of practice. If you already feel comfortable with them, great. If not, this list is here to help you get oriented early.
The goal is functional comfort, not mastery. ### Working with CSV Files (Tabular Data)
In this course, data are often provided as CSV (comma-separated values) files. CSV files are simple text-based tables used widely in research and policy work.
You should aim to be comfortable with: - Opening CSV files in Excel, Google Sheets, or similar software - Understanding that each row represents an observation and each column represents a variable - Noticing missing, inconsistent, or unexpected values - Saving or exporting CSV files without accidentally changing their structure
Helpful resources: - CSV Explainer - Data Organization in Social Sciences
These resources will also help you in your other public health courses and public health careers. They will also provide tips that will help you work together as a team.

Spreadsheet Basics (Excel or Equivalent)
You do not need advanced spreadsheet skills for this course. You do need to be able to work carefully with structured data.
You should aim to be comfortable with: - Sorting and filtering data - Understanding the difference between values and formulas - Using a small set of common functions, such as: - SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT - IF - COUNTIF, SUMIF - VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP - Basic text functions like TRIM, LEFT, RIGHT, UPPER, LOWER - Recognizing when data are missing or oddly formatted






NoteGetting Microsoft Office for Free



CSUF students are provided a subscription to Microsoft Office 365 for free. This includes Excel and also includes 50GB of storage on OneDrive. Installation Instructions.





DOT / Graphviz (Systems Representation)
You may see references to .gv files in this course. These are plain-text files used to represent systems diagrams in a structured way.
You are not expected to understand or work with dot files yet. They will be introduced later in the systems thinking module For now, it is enough to recognize the format and know that it is something we will return to.


Research in Health Care and Public Health
Students are expected to be proficient in researching topics and issues and policies in public health and health sciences. Please refer to the Research Resources module for a refresher.


Week 0 Self-Check (Not Submitted)
You do not need to turn this in. This is just a way to check your own readiness.
See how many of these you can do comfortably:

I can open a CSV file and explain what the rows and columns represent.
I can spot at least one potential issue in a dataset (missing values, inconsistent labels, strange entries).
I can sort and filter data in a spreadsheet without breaking anything.
I can explain what a simple Excel formula is doing.
I can read a DOT file and describe, in plain language, what each arrow is claiming.
I understand that these tools are being used to help me think clearly about systems, not to test my technical ability.

If several of these feel unfamiliar, that’s okay. It’s a signal to spend a bit of time with the resources above early in the term. ### Final Note on Technical Competencies

title: 2.2 System Maps
text:
A system map is a structured representation of how key elements of a system interact to produce patterns of behavior over time.
A system map is not a picture of everything. It is a deliberate abstraction that includes only those elements and relationships necessary to explain why a problem persists, changes, or reappears.






CautionSystem maps have boundaries and are not “complete pictures”



A system map has a boundary, chosen by the analyst, that determines which topics and areas are left out. It is also an abstraction shaped by a particular question. In short: a system map can contain biases and important missing pieces.


System maps focus on:

Elements — the parts of a system
Interconnections — how changes in one element influence another
Feedback loops — closed paths where effects feed back on causes
Dynamics over time — not just static structure

What distinguishes a system map from a flowchart or concept map is its explicit concern with behavior over time. System maps are used to understand:

why problems recur
why interventions produce unintended consequences
why systems resist change or amplify it

In the language of Donella Meadows, a system map helps make system structure visible—the arrangement of elements and interconnections that gives rise to observed patterns.






NoteSystem Map Definition



A system map is a simplified model that shows how interacting elements and feedback loops produce the behavior of a system over time.

Polarity and Polarity Notation
In a system map, polarity describes the direction of influence between two elements. It indicates how a change in one element affects another, all else equal.
Polarity does not describe whether an effect is good or bad, desirable or undesirable. It describes only the direction of change.

Positive Polarity (+)
A relationship has positive polarity when:

an increase in the source element leads to an increase in the target element, or
a decrease in the source element leads to a decrease in the target element.

In other words, the two elements move in the same direction.

Negative Polarity (-)
A relationship has negative polarity when:

an increase in the source element leads to a decrease in the target element, or
a decrease in the source element leads to an increase in the target element.

The two elements move in opposite directions.

What Polarity Does Not Mean

Polarity is not about moral value (+ does not mean “good”; - does not mean “bad”).
Polarity is not about strength or certainty. A + or - relationship can be weak, delayed, or conditional.
Polarity is not correlation. Polarity represents a causal claim that must be justified.



Polarity and Feedback Loops
Polarity becomes especially important in feedback loops.

A loop with an even number (or zero) of negative links is reinforcing.
A loop with an odd number of negative links is balancing.

This rule applies regardless of how many positive links are present.


Notation Conventions
In this course:

Delays are noted explicitly with || (for example, + ||).
Polarity should be assigned only when the causal direction is defensible.

Guiding Principle
Polarity encodes how a system behaves, not how we feel about it. Getting polarity right matters more than getting everything into the map.

title: 2.2 System Maps
text:
Feedback Loops
A feedback loop is a pattern where a change in something leads to effects that eventually circle back and influence that same thing again. Instead of causes and effects moving in a straight line, they form a loop. These loops help explain why problems grow, shrink, or keep repeating over time. Some feedback loops make changes bigger and faster, while others slow things down or keep them in balance. Understanding feedback loops helps explain why systems often behave in ways that are hard to predict or control.
At its simplest, a feedback loop is any closed path you can trace with the arrows and return to where you started:








feedback

Element B

Element B

+

+






Figure 7: A feedback loop: effects circle back to influence their own cause.






Balancing Loop
A balancing loop is a feedback structure that counteracts change and pushes the system toward stability or a limit. In a balancing loop, an increase in one element triggers responses that reduce that increase, while a decrease triggers forces that restore it. Balancing loops are responsible for regulation, equilibrium, and constraint. They often involve delays, thresholds, or capacity limits, which can cause overshoot or oscillation. Examples include congestion reducing travel speed, user fatigue reducing engagement, or staffing shortages limiting service delivery even as demand rises.
A thermostat is the classic example. Trace the loop: it contains exactly one negative link (an odd number), which makes it balancing.

Reinforcing Loop
A reinforcing loop is a feedback structure in which a change in one element sets off a chain of effects that amplifies that original change over time. In a reinforcing loop, growth leads to more growth, or decline leads to further decline. These loops are responsible for escalation, runaway dynamics, and path dependence. They do not require intent or coordination—once the structure is in place, the loop reinforces whatever direction the system is already moving. Examples include compounding wealth, increasing traffic demand after road expansion, or intensified police surveillance producing more data that justifies further surveillance.
Here is a surveillance example. Every link is positive (zero negative links, an even number), which makes the loop reinforcing.

section: Common Failure Modes in Systems Mapping
text:
Common Failure Modes in Systems Mapping
Not all systems maps are equally useful. Common failure modes include maps that list many variables without clear causal logic, maps that are effectively linear chains with no feedback loops, and maps that mix normative claims about what should happen with descriptive claims about what does happen. Other weak maps attempt to explain everything at once, resulting in diagrams that are visually complex but analytically shallow. Effective systems maps are selective, causal, and disciplined. Their purpose is not completeness, but explanatory power.

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: What systems thinking is really for
text:
What systems thinking is really for
Systems thinking is used to explain persistence, recurrence, and unintended consequences, not to make precise predictions. If a problem keeps returning after repeated fixes, the cause is usually system structure, not ignorance, incompetence, or bad intent. Systems thinking asks why this keeps happening, not just what happened.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: What a system map is (and is not)
text:
What a system map is (and is not)
A system map is a deliberate simplification, not a comprehensive picture. Trying to include everything makes the map meaningless. Lists of factors are not systems—relationships create systems. Diagrams are not the analysis; they are tools that support reasoning.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
text:
Elements should usually be stocks
Most elements should represent conditions that exist at a point in time, not one-time actions or events. If an element sounds like a verb (“building,” “expanding,” “enforcing”), it usually needs to be renamed as a stock (“capacity,” “rate,” “level”). Stocks give systems memory, which explains delay and resistance to change.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: Arrows represent causal claims, not associations
text:
Arrows represent causal claims, not associations
Each arrow means: a change in A causes a change in B, all else equal. Correlation alone is not sufficient. You should be able to explain the mechanism. If a relationship is uncertain, document that uncertainty rather than guessing.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: Polarity is about direction, not value
text:
Polarity is about direction, not value
A + does not mean good. A – does not mean bad. Polarity only indicates whether two elements move in the same or opposite directions. Getting polarity right matters more than making the diagram look polished.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
text:
Feedback loops are the point
A feedback loop exists when effects circle back to influence their own causes. Reinforcing loops amplify change and create growth, escalation, or collapse. Balancing loops resist change and create limits, stability, or oscillation. Most real systems contain both types of loops operating at the same time.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: Data is often endogenous to systems
text:
Data is often endogenous to systems
Many systems generate the very data used to govern them. Increased measurement or surveillance often produces more recorded problems, even when underlying conditions are unchanged. Data does not always describe reality; sometimes it helps create it.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: Short-term success can cause long-term failure
text:
Short-term success can cause long-term failure
If an intervention works briefly and then stops working, that is a systems signal, not a contradiction. Systems adapt to interventions. A useful rule of thumb: If today’s solution changes tomorrow’s problem, systems thinking is required.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: Reductionist and systems approaches are complementary
text:
Reductionist and systems approaches are complementary
Analytic methods are excellent for answering: Does this intervention work under specific conditions? Systems thinking is necessary to answer: What happens over time once the system adapts? The mistake is not using reductionist tools—it is using them outside the domain where they work.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
text:
Messy diagrams are diagnostic
If a map is unreadable, the causal structure is probably unclear. Layout problems often reflect analytic problems. Clarifying the system usually improves the diagram more than adjusting software settings.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: Delays matter more than people expect
text:
Delays matter more than people expect
Many system responses are slow, even when causes are immediate. Delays explain overshoot, frustration, and policy whiplash. Ignoring delays leads to repeated fixes that make problems worse.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: Boundary choices are part of the analysis
text:
Boundary choices are part of the analysis
No system map is complete. What you leave out determines what the system can explain. Thoughtful exclusion is a sign of rigor, not weakness.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: Structure produces outcomes—even without bad actors
text:
Structure produces outcomes—even without bad actors
Harmful outcomes do not require malicious intent. Systems can behave rationally at the local level and fail at the global level. Systems thinking shifts attention from blame to structure without abandoning responsibility.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
section: Diagrams should serve reasoning, not aesthetics
text:
Diagrams should serve reasoning, not aesthetics
Visual polish is not the goal. Color, layout, and labels should carry analytic meaning, not decoration. If a visual choice does not support reasoning, it should be removed.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.3 Systems Thinking Tips
text:
The ultimate learning goal
The goal is not mastering terminology or software.
The goal is the shift from asking: Who failed? or What should we fix? to asking: What structure makes this outcome likely?
If you can make that shift, you are doing systems thinking.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

Brief Memo (Summary of Your Research Activity)
This document explains how your team used research to test, refine, and revise your system map. It is not a literature review and not an argument about policy solutions. Its job is to make your reasoning process legible.
Your summary should be annotated and include citations to the most important sources you relied on.
Your summary must address the following:

Why those areas mattered structurally to the system

2. Evidence that shaped the system Describe how specific sources influenced your map. For each major change or confirmation, explain:

What evidence you found
How that evidence changed, clarified, or reinforced the structure of the system

3. Revisions to elements and relationships Explain:

Which causal relationships became more precise
Where you revised direction, polarity, or feedback structure

Focus on why the system now looks the way it does.
4. Remaining uncertainty and limits of evidence Identify:

Relationships that remain where the evidence is weak
Assumptions you could not fully test
Areas where evidence was contradictory, thin, or contested

Uncertainty is expected. Naming it accurately is part of the work.
5. Key sources Provide citations for the most important relevant and reliable sources that shaped your thinking.
You are being evaluated on use, not quantity.


Team Checkpoint 2 (Individual Check-In)
This is an individual, private submission — not a team deliverable. It is graded for completion/understanding and is not shared with your teammates. By this point loop ownership is individual, so this checkpoint tests your depth on the loop you personally own, plus whether research actually changed anything in it.

The skill draft is ungraded at this stage — this is your first, low-stakes attempt before Module 6, where you’ll write a stronger version of the same kind of artifact for a grade. This page collects practical advice for navigating PUBH 402. None of this replaces assignment instructions. Think of it as field notes from people who have already walked this terrain.

How to Make This Course Easier (Not Harder)
The single most useful tip in this course is this:
Focus on understanding the health problem, not on “getting the assignment right.”
Students often struggle when they:

try to reverse-engineer what the instructor wants,
treat the system map as a technical task,
aim for polish or certainty too early.

The course becomes more manageable when you:

stay curious about why the problem persists,
explore causes even when you’re unsure,
follow questions that genuinely interest you,
treat the system map as a tool for thinking, not a final answer.

If you are engaged with the health problem itself, the assignments usually take care of themselves.


Why You Can’t Save This for the End
This is the most important practical warning on this page.
A systems map is built through iteration, not assembly. Iteration means to repeat the process over and over, generating a new and better version each times. You identify elements, connect them, notice the connections don’t quite work, research, and revise — over weeks. There is no version of this course where you skip the weekly work and reconstruct a good map in the final days. The reasoning literally cannot be compressed into a single sitting.
The arithmetic makes this concrete. This is a 3-unit course, which assumes about 9 hours of work per week. If you do nothing for three weeks and then face a deadline, that’s 30+ hours of work in one week — work that depends on thinking you haven’t done yet. That isn’t a motivation problem. It’s a physical impossibility on top of your other courses and commitments.
What actually works:

Start each module early, even if you only have a vague idea.
Expect your first version to be incomplete and wrong. That’s normal and part of the process.
Treat each week’s work as raw material for the next, not as a separate task to finish.







Warning



If you find yourself planning to “catch up this weekend” on several weeks of mapping work, that plan will not survive contact with reality. Reach out before the deadline, not after.




How to Know If You’re Doing Okay
Early in the course, many students worry that they are behind. Use these signals instead:

Confused but working? That’s normal.
Asking “why does this behave this way?” You’re on track.
Revising your thinking over time? That’s success in this course.
Avoiding the work because it feels unclear? That’s a sign to pause and reach out.

There are two different states that can both feel like “I’m struggling,” and they call for opposite responses:

Confusion + engagement is productive. If you’re actively wrestling with the problem, keep going — this is the work.
Silence + avoidance is a warning sign. If you’ve stopped opening the file because it feels unclear, that’s the moment to act, not wait. Reassurance that “confusion is normal” is not permission to keep waiting.

If you recognize yourself in that second state, the single best move is to reach out, even with nothing more than “I’ve stalled and I’m not sure why.”






Warning



The students who get into trouble are rarely the confused ones — they’re the ones who went quiet and did not reach out for help.




Common Traps to Avoid
These patterns make the course harder than it needs to be:

Waiting for full clarity before starting
Over-polishing early work
Treating early drafts as if they must be “right”
Dividing team work before thinking together (see A Note on Teams)
Optimizing for format instead of explanation
Being vague when the assignment rewards specificity (see below)

These are understandable habits from other courses — but they don’t work well here.


Render Your File Before You Submit It (The Format Check)
Starting in Module 4, every .gv file you submit — the Revised System Map (Module 4), the Final System Map (Module 5), and the Final System Map (Module 7) — goes through a Format Check before anything else. Two requirements: the file has to actually render as a valid graph, and you have to submit a copy of the rendered image along with it.






ImportantZero Points for a Failed Format Check



If either check fails — the file doesn’t render, or there’s no rendered image — that component is zero points. There is no partial credit, and strong reasoning inside a file that doesn’t render can’t be evaluated, let alone rescue the score. In Module 7 specifically, since the final map is the module’s only deliverable, failing the Format Check zeroes the entire module.


This is the most avoidable kind of point loss in the whole course, because it’s mechanical, not a judgment call:

Render your file in an online Graphviz tool before you submit — see the DOT/GV Explainer for recommended tools.
Do this every time you edit the file, not just once at the start — a file that rendered last week can break with one bad edit.
If you’re starting a new .gv file, build from the Systems Map Template rather than from scratch — its structure and styling are already known to render, so you’re only responsible for what you add.
Submit the rendered image alongside the file every time. A file that renders but arrives with no image still fails the check.



Be Specific (This Is Where Most Points Are Won or Lost)
The most common problem in submitted work is vagueness: writing that could apply to almost any health problem in the U.S. A check-in or memo that talks generally about “social determinants” or “policy and financing” doesn’t show how your team’s system actually works. This is the exact standard your Team Check-In grades against — generic language is treated as indistinguishable from not understanding the system, regardless of how confident it sounds.
The fix is to name concrete elements and relationships from your own map.
Compare:

Too abstract: “Policy and financing influence outcomes.”
Specific: “Our inclusion of Medicaid reimbursement rates connects to primary care capacity, which then affects emergency department utilization. Access to primary care reduces emergency department visits, which in turn reduces wait times and improves patient outcomes.”

The second version shows reasoning. The first could have been written without doing any of the work and can be easily applied to any problem in the U.S. health care system. Whenever you’re asked what you think, point at specific elements, relationships, feedback loops, or boundary choices in your map. Uncertainty is expected; vagueness is not.


Using AI as an Adversarial Critic (Modules 5–6)
Starting in Module 5, part of the assignment design asks you to use AI differently than you might be used to: not to help you write, but to challenge your own reasoning. You’ll draft a critique skill — written instructions telling AI exactly what to check for — and use it to pressure-test a specific causal claim in your own loop. In Module 6 this becomes a full memo → AI critique → response cycle, and the critique skill itself is graded on its rigor.
This is a different skill than brainstorming or drafting with AI, and it’s easy to get wrong in either direction: too trusting (accepting whatever AI says as correct) or too dismissive (waving off a real problem because the AI’s tone was blunt). Read the AI Explainer before you get to Module 5 — it covers what AI is and isn’t good for, how to prompt it to actually disagree with you instead of defaulting to agreement, and how to draft and test a critique skill that’s rigorous rather than soft.


A note on questions, confusion, and communication
This course is designed to challenge how you think about public health problems. As a result, there will be times when you feel uncertain, confused, or unsure how to proceed — especially early in the term.
That experience is expected.
In this course, confusion is not a failure and it is not something to wait out. It is often the first signal that you are engaging with systems thinking rather than memorization or procedure.
You do not need to have a fully formed question in order to reach out. “I’m not sure what I’m missing,” “I don’t know how to improve this,” or “I feel stuck” are all sufficient reasons to contact me or come to office hours.
Waiting until the end of the term to raise questions makes it much harder to resolve them. Early, partial, and even inarticulate questions are strongly encouraged and will be treated as a normal part of learning in this course.


What to Do When You’re Stuck
Being stuck is part of systems thinking. Try this sequence:

Name what you don’t understand. Write it down, even if it’s vague.
Return to the health problem. Ask: What am I trying to explain? Why does this problem persist?
Check whether your map is doing work. Does it help you ask better questions, or is it just sitting there?
Reach out early. You do not need a fully formed question. Confusion is enough.



Where to Ask Questions
This course uses different tools for different purposes. Knowing where to go makes things much easier.

Canvas is for rules: deadlines, submissions, grades.
This website is for meaning: course content, explanations, and guidance.

So:

If you’re confused about what something means, start with this website.
If you’re confused about what is due or how to submit, check Canvas.
If you’re stuck, unsure how to proceed, or don’t have a fully formed question, reach out to me directly.







TipHigh value tip



Misrouting a question is always better than staying silent. Confusion is enough reason to ask.




A Note on Teams
Teams work best when:

thinking happens together before tasks are divided,
communication is explicit and regular,
concerns are raised early.

The trap to avoid: divide and assemble. The most common team failure is splitting the map into pieces — one person takes financing, another takes workforce, another takes structural factors — and stitching the parts together at the end. Systems analysis does not work this way.
This assignment is not like baking a cake where each person prepares one ingredient. It is closer to studying an ecosystem. You cannot assign one person the forest, another the river, and another the animals, then combine them later. The forest changes the river. The river changes the animals. The animals change the forest. The value of a systems map comes from understanding those relationships — which means the team has to think about the system together, not just merge separate sections.
A shared Graphviz file makes division of labor easy, which is exactly why it’s dangerous: the file can look complete while no one actually understands how the whole thing fits together. Build shared understanding first; divide specific tasks only after.
Module 3 requires your team to build at least one provisional feedback loop together before Module 4 splits loop ownership among individuals — so “divide and assemble” isn’t just bad practice, it works against the module’s own structure. A team that assigns loops before finding them together will have nothing to assign.
If something isn’t working:

that information matters,
escalation is responsible, not a failure,
waiting usually makes things harder.

Team friction is not a sign of a bad team — it’s often a sign that the system is doing real work.






TipAn Unresponsive Teammate Is Not a Reason to Stop



Don’t pause the whole project waiting on a teammate who’s gone quiet. Concretely:

Message them through at least two channels (e.g., email and whatever your team uses day-to-day).
Give them a specific, reasonable deadline to respond — not an open-ended wait.
If they miss it, keep moving on the parts of the map you can move on without them.
Email me if the silence continues past that deadline, and note it in your next check-in. Documenting the attempt is what protects you — and your teammate — from being penalized for someone else’s non-participation.





How Grading Works Here (Briefly)
Grades in this course are based on:

quality of reasoning appropriate to the stage of the project,
clarity of explanation,
evidence of learning and revision over time.

Grades are not based on:

early certainty,
confidence,
polish in early drafts,
having the “right” answer.

Late learning still counts.


How to Interpret Your Grades
In this course, grades are signals, not verdicts.

An early lower score usually means: your reasoning isn’t fully developed yet.
A later higher score usually means: your thinking deepened or became clearer.
Consistent engagement and revision matter more than getting everything right the first time.

If you receive feedback, the most useful question to ask is not “Why did I lose points?” but:

What part of my reasoning needs to be clearer or better supported at this stage?



A Final Tip
If this course feels hard, ask yourself:

Am I trying to manage the assignment, or am I trying to understand the health problem?

Shifting your focus back to the problem usually makes the next step clearer.
You are not expected to have everything figured out. You are expected to stay curious, engaged, and willing to revise your thinking.
That is enough to succeed here.

text:
Developing a Team Agreement
This course is designed as a problem-based learning (PBL) course. PBL is an approach that teaches a topic by trying to solve real-world problems. You are going to learn the basics of the US health care system by trying to solve a real-world health problem. PBL relies on you working effectively on a team together.
Problem-based learning requires teams to think together, not simply divide tasks and stitch them together later. Strong teams create explicit agreements about how they will work, communicate, make decisions, and hold each other accountable. This page outlines the practices that consistently lead to successful teams—and the pitfalls that undermine them.
Use this page as a reference as you develop your team’s working agreement.

Why Team Agreements Matter
A team agreement is a shared document that makes expectations explicit. It helps prevent misunderstandings, diffuses tension before it builds, and gives the team an anchor when challenges arise. Think of it as the operating manual your group writes for itself.


Core Elements of Effective Teamwork
1. Shared Understanding Comes First Before dividing tasks, the team must discuss the problem together. Everyone should understand the goals, the rationale behind your approach, and the key decisions. A strong project always begins with a shared analysis.
2. Communication Must Be Reliable and Transparent Good teams don’t rely on luck or last-minute scrambling. Establish norms such as:
• What communication platform you will use • Expected response times • How you will document decisions and who will do it • Frequency and format of check-ins Consistent communication prevents most problems.
3. Collaboration Beats “Divide and Assemble” Teams that simply split up the project produce fragmented, inconsistent work. Instead:
• Plan the structure and argument together • Review each member’s work as a group • Revise collaboratively so the final product speaks with one voice This approach mirrors real-world team-based problem solving.
4. Accountability Is Shared and Explicit Accountability is not punishment—it is clarity. A strong team agreement includes:
• Individual responsibilities and deadlines • What happens if someone falls behind • How the team will redistribute tasks when needed • How concerns will be raised and addressed Teams succeed when expectations are visible and mutual.


Building a Strong Team Agreement: Key Tips
Set Clear Roles, But Stay Flexible Assign roles such as coordinator, writer/editor, researcher, or data lead, but revisit them as the project evolves. Roles are tools, not cages.
Name Your Internal Deadlines Set earlier deadlines than the official ones. Give yourselves time to review, synthesize, and revise.
Decide How You Will Handle Conflict Conflict is normal. Avoiding it is harmful. Agree on how you will raise concerns, how disagreements will be resolved, and when to involve the instructor.
Define Quality Standards Together Clarify what “good work” means for your team. Alignment reduces frustration and mismatched expectations.
Plan for the Unexpected People get sick, overloaded, or stuck. A good agreement includes what the team will do—not who to blame—when things change.


Common Pitfalls to Avoid
Teams typically struggle when they:
• Split the project into isolated parts without shared discussion • Rely on one or two members to carry the work • Assume “someone else” is handling a task • Fail to communicate early when problems arise • Wait until the last minute to coordinate
These issues are preventable when the team agreement is clear, specific, and used actively—not just created and forgotten.


Using the Agreement Throughout the Project
A team agreement is a living document. Revisit it regularly:
• At the start of each major project phase • When challenges emerge • When team roles or needs shift
Successful teams adjust their agreements as they learn more about how they work together.

section: Guidance: How to think about leverage points
text:
Guidance: How to think about leverage points
A leverage point is a place in a system where a small or focused change could lead to a meaningful shift in how the system behaves over time. Leverage points are not necessarily the biggest or most visible parts of the system. In fact, they are often easy to overlook.
A useful way to think about leverage is to ask:
If this part of the system changed, what else would have to change as a result?
Leverage points tend to show up in places where:

Many causal pathways pass through a single element or relationship
A feedback loop could be weakened, strengthened, or redirected
A constraint limits what the system can do, even when there is effort or money
A delay causes well-intended actions to appear ineffective in the short term

Importantly, leverage points are structural, not performative. Adding more effort to an existing activity is usually not leverage. Changing the rules, incentives, information flows, or relationships that shape behavior often is.






TipThis should be familiar!



Review the materials from Module 2 on Systems Thinking, particularly the material on leverage points.


For example, expanding access to a service may matter less than changing who qualifies for it. Increasing funding may matter less than changing how funds are allocated. Education campaigns may matter less than the conditions that make certain choices rational or unavoidable in the first place.
You are not expected to find the leverage point. Systems often have multiple, competing leverage points, each with tradeoffs and limits. What matters is that you can explain, using your system map, why a particular point has leverage and what kind of change it could realistically produce.

This module uses the full version of a mechanism you’ve already practiced in lighter form in Module 5. The sequence is:

Draft a critique skill — a specific, written set of instructions for an AI tool that says exactly what it should check for in your memo.
Run your memo through your skill and get an AI critique back.
Write your response to that critique — what it got right, what it got wrong, and how (if at all) your thinking changes as a result.

See the AI Explainer for how to draft a critique skill that’s actually rigorous, and how to tell a real critique from a superficial one. The grading principle throughout: your response is the gradeable reasoning artifact — never the AI exchange itself, and never proof that you used AI.

title: Module 6 - Interpretation and Leverage (2 Weeks)
text:
1. Individual Leverage Memo
An analytical write-up of your interpretation of the system and its leverage points — not a proposal or policy brief. Use clear headings. Include, in order:

System behavior and dynamics
Describe how your system behaves based on its structure.
Focus on questions like:

What patterns does the system produce over time?
Which outcomes seem persistent or difficult to change?
What feedback loops, delays, or constraints help explain this behavior?

This section should rely on structural explanation, not storytelling or individual blame. Claims should be grounded in specific features of your team’s map.


Interpretation: why the system behaves this way
Explain why the system produces the outcomes you described.
Here, you should connect: elements → relationships → feedback loops → outcomes.
Strong interpretations make explicit causal arguments (for example, “Because X reinforces Y, the system tends to…”). Avoid listing problems or restating the map without explanation.


Identification of leverage points
Identify one to three leverage points in your system.
For each leverage point:

Describe where it sits in the system
Explain why this point has leverage, using your system map as evidence

Leverage points should be structural. You are not required to propose a full intervention, but you should make clear what would be different if this part of the system changed.


Constraints and limits
Briefly discuss what limits change in this system. This might include political or institutional constraints, resource limitations, delays that weaken short-term impact, or feedback loops that resist change.

Format
PDF or Word document. Times New Roman, 10pt, 1.5 spacing. Include your name, team, and section.


Length
750–1000 words.

title: Module 1 - Topic List
text:
Find your topic from the list below. Your topic was assigned by me to the team.


Preventable illness and death persist because vaccine uptake emerges from interacting systems of trust, access, information, and policy rather than individual choice alone. How can we stabilize and improve vaccine uptake?
Example outcome or marker: Vaccination coverage rates stratified by geography, race or ethnicity, and insurance status.



Opioid-related morbidity and mortality continue as prescribing practices, drug supply dynamics, economic conditions, and treatment access reinforce one another across health and social systems. How can we reduce death and injury from opioid overdose?
Example outcome or marker: Opioid overdose death rates per 100,000 population, examined over time.



Mental health needs go unmet because financing structures, workforce availability, stigma, and care delivery models fail to align with population demand. How could we improve access to mental health care?
Example outcome or marker: Percentage of adults with a diagnosed mental health condition who receive any mental health treatment in a given year.



Spanish-speaking communities experience worse health outcomes due to language barriers, immigration-related fear, and institutional practices that limit meaningful access to care. How can we improve access for Spanish-speaking communities.
Example outcome or marker: Percentage of Spanish-speaking adults with a usual source of care; Rate of avoidable emergency department use among Spanish-speaking patients.



Reproductive health outcomes are increasingly shaped by legal, geographic, and institutional constraints rather than clinical need or patient preference. How can we increase access?
Example outcome or marker: Average travel distance or time required to obtain comprehensive reproductive health services including abortion care.



Heat-related illness and death increase as housing quality, urban design, labor protections, and emergency response systems fail to adapt to rising temperatures.
Example outcome or marker: Heat-related emergency department visits or mortality during extreme heat events.



Emergency department congestion persists as upstream access failures, payment incentives, staffing constraints, and patient flow dynamics reinforce reliance on acute care.
Example outcome or marker: Average emergency department length of stay or inpatient boarding time.



Preventable maternal harm continues due to structural racism, fragmented prenatal care, insurance instability, and variation in hospital quality.
Example outcome or marker: Maternal morbidity rates per 10,000 delivery hospitalizations.

Spanish-speaking communities experience worse health outcomes due to language barriers, immigration-related fear, and institutional practices that limit meaningful access to care. How can we improve access for Spanish-speaking communities.
Example outcome or marker: Percentage of Spanish-speaking adults with a usual source of care; Rate of avoidable emergency department use among Spanish-speaking patients.



Reproductive health outcomes are increasingly shaped by legal, geographic, and institutional constraints rather than clinical need or patient preference. How can we increase access?
Example outcome or marker: Average travel distance or time required to obtain comprehensive reproductive health services including abortion care.



Heat-related illness and death increase as housing quality, urban design, labor protections, and emergency response systems fail to adapt to rising temperatures.
Example outcome or marker: Heat-related emergency department visits or mortality during extreme heat events.



Emergency department congestion persists as upstream access failures, payment incentives, staffing constraints, and patient flow dynamics reinforce reliance on acute care.
Example outcome or marker: Average emergency department length of stay or inpatient boarding time.



Preventable maternal harm continues due to structural racism, fragmented prenatal care, insurance instability, and variation in hospital quality.
Example outcome or marker: Maternal morbidity rates per 10,000 delivery hospitalizations.

title: Welcome
text:
This course is designed around an approach to learning called problem-based learning (PBL). PBL is a way of learning that emphasizes learning by doing. Instead of relying primarily on lectures, exams, and isolated exercises, PBL asks you to learn by working through a real problem and using that work to build understanding over time.
In this course, I will not be teaching you the U.S. health care system as a list of facts to memorize. Instead, I will help you learn how the system works by using it, analytically, to examine a concrete health problem. As you work through that problem, you will encounter how the U.S. health care system is organized and financed, how care is delivered across different levels, how decisions affect access, cost, and quality, and how ethical tradeoffs arise when resources and risks are distributed unevenly.
Different parts of the course assess different kinds of learning. The systems analysis project, which makes up most of the course, is where you will apply systems thinking to real-world health problems. Through this project, you will identify and explain major challenges related to access, cost, and quality; apply concepts to organizational and clinical settings; engage with ethical questions about resource distribution and risk–benefit tradeoffs; and research, synthesize, and evaluate evidence-based recommendations.
The final exam serves a different purpose. It focuses on your ability to clearly describe and explain the organization and financing of the U.S. health care system, as well as approaches to health services organization and financing across different levels of care. By the time you reach the final exam, you will have spent most of the term working inside a specific system. The exam asks you to step back and demonstrate that you can connect that experience to a broader understanding of how the U.S. health care system functions overall.
This structure is intentional. Complex systems like health care cannot be understood well through memorization alone. They require learning how to frame problems, test assumptions, evaluate evidence, and explain why some interventions are likely to succeed while others may fail or produce unintended consequences. You should expect your thinking to change over time. Early versions of your analysis may be incomplete or wrong, and revision is expected.
You should expect this course to feel different from classes that rely mainly on lectures and exams. At times, you may feel uncertain, incomplete, or like you don’t yet “have the answer.” That is not a sign that you are doing poorly. It is a sign that you are doing the work the course is designed to support. Early versions of your thinking are expected to be partial or wrong; improvement over time matters more than early certainty.
In broad terms, the course follows three steps:

Learn how to see the problem You will learn how to frame questions, define system boundaries, and recognize patterns such as feedback, delay, tradeoffs, and ethical tension.
Build and refine a tool to explore those questions You will construct and revise a systems map that makes structure explicit and helps you organize evidence and ethical considerations.
Use that tool to reason about the health problem and the U.S. health care system You will synthesize research, evaluate alternative approaches, and explain the advantages and limitations of different recommendations, while also developing a broader understanding of how the health care system is organized and financed.

By the end of the course, the goal is not that you can simply recite how the U.S. health care system works, but that you can analyze complex health problems, explain how system structure shapes outcomes, and critically evaluate proposed solutions—while also being able to clearly describe the broader organization and financing of the U.S. health care system. That combination of skills is what this course is designed to develop

title: Module 4 - System Expansion and Early Evidence (2 Weeks)
text:
Up to now, you have been building a system. In this module, you start asking questions about it.
The goal is not to make your system map prettier or bigger for its own sake. The goal is to use the map as a thinking device: to see where your assumptions strain, where causal stories are vague, and where important dynamics are missing or oversimplified. What is your map telling you, where is your map leaving you uncertain?
At this stage, a good system map is one that creates productive uncertainty. Confusion here is not a failure; it is evidence that the system is starting to behave like a system rather than a diagram.
Individual loop ownership begins now. At the end of Module 3, your team identified at least one provisional feedback loop together. Starting in this module, each team member takes individual ownership of developing one loop in depth. Loops are built so that they share elements with at least one other teammate’s loop — the point is not to give you a private corner of the map to work on alone, but to make sure that developing your loop well requires understanding how it connects to your teammates’ loops. A team that divides the map without doing this collaborative thinking will produce a map that is visibly broken, not just shallow.
