title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Elements
The things we can usually see. The elements that make up our traffic system include things like: “cars on the road,” “travel time,” “road capacity.” Elements do not have to be things one can see. They can be intangible things. e.g. “Perceived ease of driving,” “Perceived cost of driving.” We can’t see these things but they exist. Elements are nouns.1
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Interconnections
The relationships between elements (how congestion affects speed, how travel time affects demand). Some interconnections are physical flows, e.g. cars moving on the road. Some are flows of information or signals that change the behavior of a system, e.g. brake lights.2
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Purpose or function
What the system actually does, inferred from its behavior over time. A key move in systems thinking is recognizing that a system’s purpose is revealed by its outcomes, not by its stated goals. If congestion repeatedly returns after expensive interventions, that recurrence tells us something true about how the system is structured.






ImportantMeadows on seeing function or purpose



A system’s function or purpose is not necessarily spoken, written, or expressed explicitly, except through the operation of the system. The best way to deduce the system’s purpose is to watch for a while to see how the system behaves.


It is important to remember, particularly in public health or health care systems analysis, that the purpose or a function of a system is not necessarily the stated purpose or function. The purpose of a system is what it does. If that purpose doesn’t match what we expect or believe a system is doing, that is a useful point for more investigation.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Stock
A stock is an accumulation, something that can be measured at a point in time. Examples include population, infrastructure, trust, capacity, or exposure.
A stock does not have to be a physical quantity.







Stock
Health Care Example




Capacities
Number of hospital beds


Levels of access
Percentage of population with access to a hospital


Degrees of coverage
Percentage of persons in an employer-based health plan


Distributions of power
Level of trust in medical institutions


Institutional arrangements
Percentage of fee-for-service reimbursement arrangements


Accumulated risk or exposure
Total number of persons living in a high-risk area



Most people mistakenly think stocks must be “countable things.” That’s not how Meadows uses the term.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Flow
A flow is a process that increases or decreases a stock over time. Examples include births and deaths, construction and decay, funding and spending, exposure and recovery. Using our stock examples above, we can name some likely flows in a health care system.







Stock Example
Flow Example




Number of hospital beds
Construction and delay of hospital infrastructure


Percentage of population with access to a hospital
Enrollment and disenrollment from health plans


Percentage of persons in an employer-based health plan
Unemployment and employment rates


Level of trust in medical institutions
Trust-building and trust-eroding activities


Percentage of fee-for-service reimbursement arrangements
Changes in reimbursement policies


Total number of persons living in a high-risk area
Availability and affordability of housing



Stocks change slowly because flows operate over time. This gives systems memory and explains why systems often respond to interventions with delays. If we think of the example above, the number of hospital beds (a stock) changes slowly because construction and delay (flows) occur over time. Yet, the percentage of population with access to a hospital (another stock) changes more rapidly because enrollment and disenrollment (flows) can happen more frequently. So, the rate of change in a stock depends on the frequency and magnitude of its associated flows.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Stocks, Flows, and Accumulation
Systems behave the way they do because of accumulation. Some elements of a system build up over time (stocks), while others control the rate at which those stocks change (flows). Infrastructure, workforce capacity, chronic disease burden, trust, and institutional legitimacy are all examples of stocks. Funding rates, enrollment rates, exposure levels, and staffing turnover are flows. Many failed interventions target flows while ignoring the stocks they influence, leading to delayed or disappointing results. Understanding this distinction helps explain why systems often respond slowly to change and why short‑term fixes rarely resolve long‑term problems.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Balancing Feedback: Congestion Self-Limiting
A balancing loop is one that resists change and pushes the system toward a temporary equilibrium. It works by counteracting any deviation from a desired state, thereby maintaining stability. A thermostat is a classic example of a balancing loop. In our traffic example, as the number of cars increases, congestion worsens. Slower speeds increase travel time, which raises the perceived cost of driving. Some people respond by reducing trips, which lowers the number of cars. This loop resists change and pushes the system toward a temporary equilibrium.

This loop explains why congestion rarely grows without bound. This is how you draw a balancing loop.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Reinforcing Feedback: Induced Demand
A reinforcing loop is a feedback structure in which a change in one element sets off a chain of effects that amplifies that original change over time. In a reinforcing loop, growth leads to more growth, or decline leads to further decline. These loops are responsible for escalation, runaway dynamics, and path dependence. They do not require intent or coordination—once the structure is in place, the loop reinforces whatever direction the system is already moving. Examples include compounding wealth, increasing traffic demand after road expansion, or intensified surveillance producing more data that justifies further surveillance.

This is how you draw a reinforcing loop
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Delays and Structural Change
A critical insight from Meadows is the importance of delays. Delay makes the system especially hard to manage. Short-term improvements create confidence in interventions whose long-term effects undermine them. Systems with long delays often produce oscillation, overshoot, and policy frustration.







ImportantQuick test to determine if it is a system



If all of the following are true, you have a system. If not, you just have a bunch of stuff.

Can you identify parts… and
Do the parts affect each other… and
Do the parts together produce an effect that is different from the effect of each part on its own? … and perhaps
Does the effect, the behavior over time, persist in a variety of circumstances?



If we took the elements of the urban traffic system and showed the interconnections, it would make a system map:
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Analytic (Reductionist) Approaches
Analytic approaches work by isolating variables and estimating effects under controlled or simplified conditions.
They are most useful when the question asks:

What causes this specific outcome?
Does X increase or decrease Y?
How large is the effect of an intervention?
What mechanism operates in isolation?

These approaches assume: - relatively stable relationships - limited feedback - clear system boundaries - short or well-defined time horizons

Traffic examples (analytic questions)

Does adding a lane reduce average travel time in the first year?
Does synchronizing traffic lights reduce delay at an intersection?
Does a congestion alert change departure times during a heat wave?
Does a stalled vehicle increase delay on a specific corridor?

These are legitimate questions. Analytic methods are well suited to answering them.






NoteWhat are examples of analytic questions in health care?




Does a specific medication reduce blood pressure?
Does expanding clinic hours increase appointment attendance?
Does a care coordination program reduce 30-day readmissions?
Does increasing reimbursement for primary care increase visit volume?
Does a public health warning increase heat-safety behaviors in the short term?
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Systems Thinking Approaches
Systems thinking focuses on how interactions, feedback, and accumulation produce patterns of behavior over time.
It is most useful when the question asks:

Why does a problem persist?
Why do fixes backfire or lose effectiveness?
Why does the system adapt to interventions?
Why do outcomes differ across places or groups?

These approaches assume:

feedback loops
adaptation and learning
delays between cause and effect
endogenous behavior (the system changes itself)


Traffic examples (systems questions)

Why does congestion return a few years after road expansion?
Why does adding capacity increase total driving?
Why does congestion persist even when accidents are rare?
Why do travel times stabilize at a high level rather than improving?

These questions cannot be answered by isolating one variable at a time. They require understanding system structure.






NoteWhat are examples of systems questions in health care?




Why do health care costs continue to rise despite efficiency reforms?
Why do emergency departments remain crowded after expanding capacity?
Why does increasing insurance coverage not eliminate access barriers?
Why do workforce shortages persist despite higher demand?
Why do racial and socioeconomic disparities persist after policy changes?
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
How the Approaches Work Together
Analytic methods are excellent at answering:

Does this intervention work in the short term?

Systems thinking is necessary to answer:

What happens over time once the system adapts?

In the traffic case: - analytic evidence helps evaluate specific interventions - systems thinking explains why congestion persists - neither approach alone is sufficient
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Guiding Principle
The question determines the method. If the problem adapts to your solution, a systems approach is required to understand why.






TipA Practical Decision Rule



Use this simple rule: If today’s solution changes tomorrow’s problem, you need systems thinking.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
section: Changing the elements usually has the least effect on a system.
text:
Changing the elements usually has the least effect on a system.
If you change elements in a system, this will usually have little or no effect on a system. Think of Meadows’ example of the football team, “if you change all the players on a football team, it is still recognizably a football team.” We can change the players on our team and that team may play better or play worse but it will still achieve its purpose of playing football. The underlying system of a football team did not change.

“A system generally goes on being itself, changing only slowly if at all, even with complete substitutions of its elements—as long as its interconnections and purposes remain intact.” D. Meadows
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
section: Changing relationships usually changes system behavior
text:
Changing relationships usually changes system behavior
If you change how the elements relate to each other, this will change the behavior of a system. Using our football example, if we changed the rules of US football and made it against the rules to pick up the ball, the behavior of the football team would change almost immediately but it’s purpose would remain the same.
When you see a policy failure, it usually mean that the intervention was made in the wrong loop or only adjusted elements without changing system behavior.

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Where to Intervene
You must understand the system before you can intervene. If you do not understand the system, you will likely intervene in the wrong place and make the problem worse. The goal of systems thinking is to identify leverage points in a system where interventions are most likely to produce meaningful change. Leverage points are places in a system where a small change can lead to a large shift in behavior. We are looking to change the system and acheive long-term structural change. We are not looking for short-term fixes that will not change the system.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
text:
Endogenous vs. Exogenous Explanations
The goal of systems thinking is to explain outcomes as the result of internal system structure, not just external forces. While shocks such as economic downturns, pandemics, or political changes can matter, they do not by themselves explain persistent patterns. We use two different terms to describe what is internal to a system (endogenous) and what is external (exogenous).
Endogenous explanations focus on how system elements interact to produce outcomes repeatedly over time. Rather than asking what outside factor caused a problem, systems thinking asks how the system is organized such that this outcome keeps occurring. This shift is essential for moving from blame‑based explanations to structural analysis.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: 2.1 Systems Thinking
section: Leverage Points: How do we change a system?
text:
Leverage Points: How do we change a system?
Read “Leverage Points” by Meadows. This is a highly influential essay that outlines the different points we can try and change systems and ranks them based on their effectiveness in bringing change to a system.
Meadows’ leverage points are not a checklist for policy design. They are a diagnostic framework for understanding why most interventions fail and why effort is often applied in the least effective places. The leverage points are ordered from shallow to deep not by political feasibility, but by their capacity to change system behavior over time.
You do not need to memorize her list but should be familiar with it. You should internalize three ideas based on this list however:

1 - Most interventions target low-leverage points.
It feels easy, doable, and manageable to change things like parameters, funding levels, capacity, etc.—however, these interventions usually leave a system untouched. They can feel good and they are relatively easy, but they don’t accomplish much. Low-leverage public health interventions ask people to adapt to systems that refuse to change.
Some public health interventions at this level are best understood as forms of performance rather than structural change. They signal concern, responsibility, or action without substantially altering the system that produces the problem. These interventions are not useless—they may provide reassurance, visibility, or short-term benefit—but they should not be confused with strategies that change system behavior over time.
In every case of public health as performance rather than structural change:

The intervention reduces moral or political pressure
That reduction weakens momentum for structural change
The system becomes more stable and more fragile at the same time

This is why “performance” is not neutral. It’s a feedback intervention.
It is important to recognize that some interventions persist not because they work, but because they feel like action. They offer moral reassurance, professional identity reinforcement, or political cover. Systems thinking does not dismiss these effects—but it asks us to be honest about what they do and do not change.






Tip



If an intervention makes us feel better faster than it changes outcomes, it’s probably performing rather than transforming.


When an intervention does not alter power, incentives, or feedback loops, its primary effect may be to make participants feel responsible rather than to make the system behave differently.
Recognizing this does not mean rejecting these interventions outright—it means placing them accurately within a system analysis. The task of public health is not to avoid symbolic action, but to recognize when symbolism has replaced structural change.

Examples

Health education and promotion campaigns encouraging healthy eating. These interventions target individual knowledge but don’t address structural issues like food pricing, labor schedules, marketing or built environments.
Heat advisories that tell people to “check on neighbors” or “hydrate” or “stay indoors” during extreme heat. The underlying determinants of heat-related illness are untouched: housing quality, labor protections, energy affordability. These messages assume access to air conditioning, safe housing, social networks, and time flexibility.
Expanding cancer screening programs without expanding diagnostic, treatment, and follow-up ability. Screening increases the flow of information (detection) but does not change the system’s ability to respond.




2- High leverage can look abstract, slow, or political
Information flows, rules, and goals are harder to change, take longer, and feel less “actionable.” This feeling can make these interventions less likely to be implemented even though they are the most likely to actually cause a change in the system. System change requires being in it for the long-term and humans aren’t great at that.


3 - Leverage without diagnosis is reckless
You cannot choose a leverage point until you understand the dominant feedback loops.

title: DOT/GV Explainer
text:
This course uses GV files (Graphviz) as a simple, formal way to represent systems. GV is not a drawing tool. It is a text-based language for describing the elements of a system and the connections between them.
.gv is used here because it encourages precision, transparency, and clarity of thinking about system structure.






WarningClass Success Tip



Remember, we are using systems maps as tools to understand how the US healthcare system works. We will create systems maps using software. .gv files are written in a language that we will use to describe our healthcare system and create a map.


You can also follow along and look at my example .gv file on a coffee shop’s customer traffic. This file is not on Canvas — it’s downloadable from the class GitHub page (link on that page).


A .gv file is a plain-text file that describes a graph. A system map is a graph.
In a .gv file:

Elements of a system are written as nodes
Connections between elements are written as edges
Direction matters: arrows encode influence or causation

A simple .gv file might look like this:
digraph {
  Population -> Resource_Use
  Resource_Use -> Environmental_Impact
}
In plain language, this .gv file is making the following claims:

There is an element called Population.
There is an element called Resource Use.
There is an element called Environmental Impact.
Changes in Population influence Resource Use.
Changes in Resource Use influence Environmental Impact.

The arrows indicate the direction of influence. This model does not claim that environmental impact directly affects population, nor does it claim that resource use affects population in return. Those connections are absent, and that absence is itself a modeling choice.
This file describes a system structure. How it looks visually depends on how it is rendered.






ImportantUsing Text Editors (Required)



For this assignment, you will use a plain text file to describe your system map in Graphviz (.gv) format. A plain text file contains only words and symbols—no hidden formatting, fonts, or layout instructions. Text editors (such as Notepad, TextEdit in plain-text mode, or VS Code) are designed for this kind of file. We use plain text because it is transparent, stable, and precise: what you type is exactly what the system reads. This keeps the focus on causal structure and logic rather than visual design or software features. You are not being evaluated on technical skill—only on whether your system relationships are clearly and correctly specified.
Do not use Word or Google Docs for working on these files. Use only a text editor. Notepad is the free text editor that comes on Windows. Text Edit is the free text editor that comes on an Apple computer.





.gv files are used because they:

Makes assumptions explicit
Forces clarity about direction and influence
Separates system structure from visual layout
Supports feedback loops naturally
Encourages thinking in terms of elements and connections (after Donella Meadows)
Keeps you from worrying about drawing systems maps.




You do not need to memorize .gv syntax. You do need to be able to work with simple examples.
You should aim to be comfortable with:

Reading a .gv file and explaining what each node represents
Following arrows and explaining what each connection claims
Recognizing feedback loops as circular paths
Creating a .gv file for your system map using a template.
Making small edits to an existing .gv file
Understanding that layout is separate from meaning

.gv is used to support systems thinking, not to test technical skill.



.gv files support simple conventions that help make system structure clearer without changing meaning. In addition to the examples below, open my example .gv file and examine it while you read the explanations below.


Comments allow you to leave notes in a .gv file that do not affect the graph.

Single-line comments begin with //
Multi-line comments are wrapped in /* */

Comments are useful for explaining modeling choices, assumptions, or uncertainties.
Example:
// This connection represents perceived influence, not measured causation
Population -> Resource_Use



Connections can be labeled to indicate whether an influence is positive or negative.

A positive (+) polarity means that an increase in one element tends to increase the other (or a decrease tends to decrease it).
A negative (–) polarity means that an increase in one element tends to decrease the other (or vice versa).

Example:
Population -> Resource_Use [label="+"]
Resource_Use -> Environmental_Impact [label="+"]
Labels describe the direction of influence, not its strength.



Delays can be represented by labeling a connection or by inserting an intermediate element.
Example (labeled delay):
Resource_Use -> Environmental_Impact [label="+ (delay)"]
Example (explicit delay element):
Resource_Use -> Accumulated_Effects -> Environmental_Impact
Delays are important because they often explain why systems behave in unexpected or counterintuitive ways.



You will be asked to show reinforcing and balancing loops in your project. You can show those using subgraphs and clusters.
Here is an example




GV allows basic formatting to improve readability:

Labels can include spaces and explanatory text
Nodes and edges can be grouped using clusters
Visual attributes (such as color or shape) may be used sparingly for clarity

Formatting choices should support understanding, not decoration. Structure comes first.

title: Class AI Policy
text:
This page is the single canonical statement of how AI fits into PUBH 402 — how you may use it in your own work, how it’s built into specific assignments, and how I use it myself. Sections of the Syllabus cover student use and instructor use in similar terms; this page is the fuller, consolidated version, including the assignment-embedded mechanism in Modules 5–6 that the Syllabus doesn’t cover.



AI and foundation models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, and similar tools) are permitted without restriction as part of your process — brainstorming, drafting, organizing ideas, checking clarity, exploring alternatives, and supporting learning.
However, all submitted work must ultimately represent your own reasoning, judgment, and understanding. You are responsible for the accuracy, integrity, and ethical quality of anything you submit, regardless of whether AI tools were used in its creation. AI systems are known to generate incorrect information, fabricated citations, biased outputs, and other errors — reliance on AI output does not excuse mistakes or misrepresentation.
Disclosure. If you used AI tools at any point in completing an assignment, include a brief disclosure statement at the end of your submission:

I used an AI tool (name of tool, e.g., ChatGPT) to support my work on this assignment. Specifically, I used it for: [e.g., brainstorming ideas, outlining, checking clarity, generating alternative phrasings]. All analysis, interpretation, and final conclusions are my own, and I reviewed and verified any AI-assisted content for accuracy and appropriateness.

If you did not use AI tools, no disclosure is required. Failure to disclose meaningful AI use is a misrepresentation, treated as a distinct academic-integrity violation from plagiarism of human-authored work.
Limits. You may not submit work that is primarily or substantially AI-generated in place of your own thinking. Work is unacceptable if you cannot explain, defend, revise, or extend its reasoning independently of the AI tool. AI tools may not be used during examinations (Exam 1, Final Exam) — these are designed to assess individual understanding and reasoning under constraint, in conditions where external tools are unlikely to help anyway.
Used well, AI can improve the quality of your work and make learning more efficient. Used poorly, it can flatten thinking and obscure understanding. In this course, AI is treated as a collaborator — not an author, and not a substitute for intellectual responsibility.



This is different from Section 1: it is not “you may use AI” but AI built directly into two assignments, appearing in increasing weight as the term progresses. It applies only to Module 5 and Module 6 — not to the team system maps in Modules 3, 4, 5, or 7.
Module 5 (light version, ungraded practice). Each student stress-tests one causal claim in their own individually-owned loop — not the team’s whole map. As part of this, you draft a critique skill: written instructions telling the AI what to check for (e.g., unsupported causal claims, missing polarity justification, weak mechanism). This skill draft is not graded — it’s a low-stakes first attempt before the same kind of artifact is scored in Module 6. You then run your skill, get a critique back, and write a short response. The whole exercise — skill draft, critique, response — is submitted as part of the Module 5 check-in (Team Checkpoint 2), not as a separate deliverable.
Module 6 (full version, graded). A complete cycle: write an individual leverage memo, draft a critique skill (this time graded on its own rigor — a skill written to go easy on the memo scores poorly on its own terms, regardless of the critique it produces), run the memo through the skill, and write a response to the critique. Three components, 25 points total: memo (7), drafted skill (8), response to critique (10).
The constant grading principle: your response to the AI’s critique is the gradeable reasoning artifact — never the AI exchange itself, and never proof that you used AI. A student who writes a soft, superficial critique skill to avoid real scrutiny is graded down on the skill itself, which is the built-in defense against gaming this mechanism.
For practical guidance on drafting a rigorous skill, telling a real critique from a superficial one, and common AI failure modes (hallucination, fabricated statistics, sycophancy) — see the AI Explainer.



Course design. I use AI tools as part of my drafting, synthesis, and analytic workflow — supporting course design, developing rubrics, testing assessment logic, and assisting with large-scale evaluation under criteria I define and control. I remain fully responsible for all instructional, evaluative, and grading decisions; no automated system operates independently of my judgment. This disclosure models transparency about AI as an intellectual and administrative tool — it does not imply equivalence between instructor and student responsibility.
Grading support. I use AI for a first-pass review of student submissions to support my own grading. This is scoped to triage and surfacing only — never scoring: it can flag patterns, surface items for review, or help organize submissions for evaluation, but it does not assign scores or make final grading determinations. Before any student work is reviewed this way, identifying information (names, student IDs) is removed — the AI tool never sees submissions tied to your identity.
Final exam grading is scoped the same way — triage/surfacing only, not scoring — driven by legal defensibility concerns specific to a summative, individually-weighted assessment.
Student AI-use policy (Sections 1–2) governs authorship and learning; instructor AI use governs course design and evaluation. These are intentionally distinct and should not be read as parallel or equivalent.

title: System Elements
text:
Primary care visit capacity: The number of primary care appointments a community or system can supply within a given time period.
Primary care care coordination capacity: The capacity of primary care settings to coordinate referrals, follow-up, and communication across providers for a patient.
Specialty care visit capacity: The number of specialist appointments a community or system can supply within a given time period.
Specialty care referral availability: The ease or speed with which patients can obtain and complete a referral to specialty care.
Language access service availability: The availability of interpreter services, translated materials, and bilingual staff within a health care setting.

title: System Elements
text:
Federal and State Policy

Medicaid eligibility rules: The income, categorical, and documentation requirements that determine who qualifies for Medicaid coverage in a given state.
Medicare coverage rules: The federal rules that determine which services, providers, and populations are covered under Medicare.
State scope-of-practice laws: State laws defining which clinical tasks a given type of health professional (e.g., nurse practitioner, pharmacist) is legally permitted to perform.
Federal regulatory requirements: Federal rules that providers, payers, or manufacturers must follow to operate or participate in federal health programs.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: System Elements
text:
Enforcement and Accountability

Capacity for administrative processing: The volume of applications, claims, or eligibility determinations an agency or payer can process within a given time period.
Sanctions: Penalties (financial, licensing, or program-exclusion) imposed on providers, payers, or institutions for noncompliance with health regulations.
Reimbursement requirements: The documentation, coding, or procedural conditions a provider must meet before receiving payment for a service.
Administrative Staffing: The number of personnel employed to carry out administrative, eligibility, or compliance functions within an agency or institution.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: System Elements
text:
Workforce

Primary care clinician supply: The number of primary care physicians, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants available relative to population need.
Specialist clinician supply: The number of specialist physicians available relative to population need.
Nursing workforce availability: The number of registered nurses and related nursing personnel available relative to need.
Public health workforce capacity: The number of trained public health personnel available to staff public health functions.
crumbs: PUBH 402: Introduction to the US Health Care System

title: System Elements
text:
Infrastructure

Hospital bed capacity: The number of staffed hospital beds available within a given system or region.
Primary care facility availability: The number and geographic distribution of primary care clinics or practices.
Health information technology interoperability: The degree to which health information systems can exchange and use patient data across providers and institutions.
Emergency care access: The availability and proximity of emergency department or urgent care services to a population.
Obstetric/maternity care availability: The availability of labor and delivery units, obstetric clinicians, or perinatal services within a given system or region.

title: Module 7 - Synthesis and Final Submission (1 Week)
text:
This is the point where everything you’ve been building comes together.
Up to now, you’ve been mapping parts of a system, testing assumptions, revising relationships, and sitting with uncertainty. Module 7 asks you to step back and finalize your team’s system map — your best current explanation of how the system works, clear, grounded, and honest about its limits.






TipA Final Note



This module is about synthesis, not stress-testing yourself at the last minute. You are not expected to discover something new here. You are expected to make sense of what you already built.
Systems thinking is not about certainty. It’s about disciplined explanation in a messy world. This final submission is your best current explanation — clear, grounded, and honest about its limits.
Take a breath. Then finalize the system’s story.

Final System Map
